target_customer: Rare disease families, patient foundations, impact investors and pharma partners who fund drug repurposing programs
problem: Ultra-rare metabolic diseases have no commercial drug development, so families wait for treatments that no company has an incentive to build.
business_model: Joint ventures with patient families and funders (PerlQuests), planned spin-out of asset-centric development companies; later grants and foundation-funded programs
product_category: Rare disease drug repurposing biotech (yeast and patient-avatar screening)

founders.name: Ethan Perlstein
education: PhD (degree stated in the 2017 press release; school not found)
founders.background_notes: Named as founder and CEO in the November 2017 press release. YC page lists a Founders heading with no names.

technical_complexity.rationale: Building yeast and patient-derived disease models, running compound screens and moving hits into clinical trials is wet-lab biology plus regulatory work, hard for a tiny team.

defensibility.rationale: The screening workflow was published (Lao et al., 2019 per the company Substack) and each program depended on funder money, so the platform alone was not hard to copy; the PMM2-CDG clinical lead was the real asset.

takeover_risk_then.outcome: No incumbent copied the model. Novartis took part in the 2017 round under a research collaboration; the company said a licensing partner exited in 2019 and it wound down the original structure.

market_need_then: Families of children with ultra-rare diseases were organizing and funding research themselves, and drug repurposing for rare diseases had patient advocacy support; the YC description frames Perlara as a YC for rare disease parents.

branding.domain_note: perlara.com is the company domain per the YC page.

identity.visual_style: Versioned story format (Perlara 1.0, 1.5, 2.0, 3.0) with archives on the website
identity.voice_and_tone: Informal, emoji-friendly scientific storytelling on a Substack

branding.brand_signature: Numbered versions of the company (Perlara 1.0 to 3.0) and open-source data posts
branding.community_and_virality: Company Substack with Cure Odyssey posts for individual rare diseases; open data release promised for the NGLY1 PerlQuest per the 2019 RARE Daily report.

brand_strength.rationale: Known in rare disease circles through founder visibility and the company Substack, but no evidence of brand-driven growth.

pivots.from: Perlara 1.0 PerlQuest joint ventures and ArkBase platform
pivots.to: Perlara 1.5 one-person virtual clinical development company running repurposing trials at Mayo Clinic
pivots.why: Company states a licensing partner exited and financing for clinical leads could not be secured (RARE Daily, 2019).

pivots.to: Perlara 2.0 decentralized, distributed biotech with a pop-up yeast lab
pivots.why: Per the YC description and company Substack; reason not detailed.

outcome_analysis: Perlara raised a reported 7.4 million dollars in November 2017 and had reached 9.9 million total, then lost a licensing partner and could not finance its clinical leads, so it announced a wind-down in 2019. It survived as a tiny virtual company that ran epalrestat and aripiprazole repurposing trials at Mayo and later rebuilt as a yeast screening shop funded by foundations and a 2025 SBIR grant. It stalled as a venture but kept operating as a mission-driven biotech.
notes: Total raised was 9.9M by Nov 2017 per the press release, so about 2.5M of earlier funding (2016 seed per aggregators) is not recorded; no dated primary source found. CB Insights lists 10.02M over 7 rounds and a Series A in Aug 2017, VCBacked lists 1.7M total; aggregators conflict and are not recorded. The 2025 grant date is November 2025 on the company site and October 2025 on CB Insights. Competitor list left empty: the dated searches returned only company-owned material and nothing dated near Winter 2016. Founder education and prior employers not found.
